paper_title: Taking Apart and Putting Together: Tracking Objects Through Physical Transformations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), a training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via a generate-evaluate-judge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. To benchmark TTU, we curate Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), a dataset including state graphs with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA, while operating $6\times$ to $15\times$ faster than prior methods. Project page: https://davidegardenal.github.io/tipo-tracking

sections.content: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via generateevaluatejudge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. To benchmark TTU, we curate Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), dataset including state graphs with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA, while operating 6 to 15 faster than prior methods. Project page: davidegardenal.github.io/tipo-tracking 1. Introduction Imagine someone preparing Moka pot (Fig. 1, t1): they unscrew the collector (t2), pull out the funnel filter (t3), and set the components aside. In matter of seconds, single object splits into three distinct parts. Modern visual foundation trackers (e.g., SAM 2 [26], SAM 3 [6]) are built around entity persistence: they follow objects through complex motion, but have no mechanism to revise identities when objects physically divide or merge. As shown in the last row of Fig. 1 (SAM 2.1), the tracker either stubbornly preserves single ID across split (t2) or arbitrarily drops fragmented parts (t3, t4). Reassembling the pot (t4, t5) reverses the ambiguity: should the tracker follow separate components or recognize unified Moka pot again? Yet the physical world is inherently dynamic [30, 32], with objects routinely assembled, disassembled, sliced, and folded [11, 15]. Maintaining pixel tracklets is only half the challenge; dynamic environments require system that tracks objects through transformations, describes the physical process, and updates identities and partwhole relationships over time [19, 40]. To address this dynamic scenario, we formalize the task of Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU). Given video and initial object prompts, TTU system must (i) track objects through assemblies and disassemblies, (ii) describe the physical transformations, (iii) update tracklet IDs and semantic labels, and (iv) keep track of how every object relates to its parts over time. The output is single, unified state graph paired with object masks (Fig. 1, TIPO row). This structured representation naturally enables several downstream applications: robots can verify step completion before planning actions [23], and AR assistants can monitor current assembly states to guide users [24]. Prior work only partially addresses this task. TubeletGraph [29] handles isolated split events but has three major limitations for TTU (Fig. 1, second row). First, its search for parts triggers only after track loss, missing the initial split (t2) and detecting only later fragmentation (t3). Second, it is restricted to disassemblies and cannot model assemblies, causing identity switches (t4) and failing to resolve assemblies (t5). Lastly, tracking dense candidate regions across the whole scene incurs severe overhead (0.2 FPS). We take fundamentally different approach. Our key observation is simple: split and merge events are observable in the current frames geometry. In Fig. 1, the collectors separation is instantly evident at t2 because the tracked mask fragments into disconnected components. There is no need to scan through the video to recover lost parts; the visual evidence is already in the frame. Building on this, we introduce Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), training-free framework for TTU that explicitly models both assemblies and disassemblies on top of foundation trackers. At each frame, TIPO executes generateevaluatejudge pipeline. It first generates split and merge state proposals by Table 1. Comparison between VISTA and VOST-TAS datasets. Next, it evaluates each state proposal against promptable mask-decoder priors using complementary inner and external overlap metrics, distinguishing genuine transformations from visual occlusions without expensive search. Finally, Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) [14, 25] judges whether the top-scoring proposal matches the visual evidence in the frame and, if so, assigns semantic labels to the action and the newly formed objects (e.g., Remove and Moka filter). By querying the MLLM only on structurally validated proposals, TIPO continuously updates the state graph without compromising tracking speed. To evaluate TTU, we introduce Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), challenging benchmark of 50 multi-object videos (26K+ frames) featuring dense state-graph annotations across 256 distinct transformations. Unlike VOST-TAS [29], which covers only disassemblies, VISTA includes 124 assemblies and more than doubles the annotated transformations (Tab. 1). Crucially, the state graphs enable rigorous structural evaluation of each transformation, whereas VOST-TAS annotates only resulting parts,ignoring which object transformed and rewarding methods that over-predict transformations (Tab. 3). Contributions. Our core contributions are: i) We formalize the TTU task, extending prior tracking paradigms [29] to model both object assemblies and disassemblies. ii) We propose TIPO, training-free framework that replaces dense spatiotemporal search [29] with per-frame geometric evaluation of state proposals using mask-decoder priors, backed by sparse MLLM validation and semantic labeling. iii) We curate VISTA, the first benchmark to provide comprehensive state-graph annotations for both assembly and disassembly. iv) We show through extensive experiments that TIPO establishes new state-of-the-art for tracking and state-graph accuracy, while running 6 to 15 faster than competitors. 2. Related Work Object Tracking and Foundation Models. Traditional multi-object tracking and video object segmentation primarily rely on tracking-by-detection [3, 5, 38] and tracking-byquery [21, 28, 37] paradigms. While accurate, these methods often struggle with target deformation and scale variation, and require extensive annotated training data [9, 34]. To address these issues, recent work leverages foundation models Figure 2. Overview of TIPO. At each frame It, the tracker provides the set of per-object masks. The pipeline operates in four stages (14): (1) extraction of the disjoint components and mask sampling, (2) generation of all possible assembly and disassembly states, (3) evaluation of the state proposals based on mask overlap metrics, (4) validation of the highest-scoring proposal by the MLLM Judge and semantic labeling. Lastly, the state graph and the tracker are updated with the validated state. such as SAM [16] for zero-shot instance association [18], interactive tracking [9, 34], and unified real-time tracking with streaming memory in SAM 2 [26]. SAM 3 further extends this line to Promptable Concept Segmentation by decoupling recognition and localization [6]. However, these models still assume structural integrity: identity tracking breaks down when objects fragment or merge. While recent human-inthe-loop systems mitigate this via online correction [35], they remain annotation tools rather than autonomous models. In contrast, we explicitly model structural transformations. By repurposing SAMs zero-shot segmentation priors, i.e. sampling internal mask representations, we isolate the structural cues needed to autonomously track split and merge events, eliminating the need for human intervention or domain-specific fine-tuning. Understanding Object Transformations. Recent literature explores physical state changes in videos. Early work targeted human-driven events in egocentric datasets [11, 15], introducing benchmarks like VOST [30] and VSCOS [36]. Subsequent work pursued fine-grained understanding: VidOSC temporally localizes open-world transformations [32], while SPOC spatially segments progressive changes [20] for robotic manipulation [19]. Most recently, Sun et al. [29] bridged state recognition and tracking via the Track Any State task and VOST-TAS benchmark. Their TubeletGraph framework tracks all candidate regions of the scene as tubelets and, after transformation, filters them with semantic and spatial priors to decide which belong to the target. However, tracking the whole scene is computationally heavy, and the framework is strictly limited to disassembly events. In contrast, TIPO natively models both assemblies and disassemblies. By evaluating state proposals via per-frame spatial overlap, we achieve accurate transformation tracking at fraction of the computational cost. MLLMs for Understanding Object Transformations. Recent MLLMs, including both closed-source models [1, 13, 22] and open-weight architectures [14, 25], have shown strong capabilities in parsing long-context video, enabling the grounding of dynamic physical properties, causality, and structural changes [17, 39]. For tracking transformations, prior work primarily used MLLMs as offline pseudo-label generators for training [32] or as post-hoc captioners to extract textual descriptions from mask-contoured keyframes [29]. In contrast, our pipeline integrates an MLLM to validate state changes directly within the tracking loop, effectively filtering out implausible false positives. 3. Methodology 3.1. Unlike single-object tracking formulations that assume all resulting entities derive from single progenitor, TTU naturally models arbitrary multi-object interactions, where distinct entities can independently persist, split into parts, or merge to form new objects. t1, vi

While prior benchmarks like VOST-TAS [29] consider state changes, they annotate only the resulting parts rather than modeling the transformation process itself. As summarized in Tab. 1, VISTA comprises 50 diverse sequences sourced from Assembly101 [27], IKEA ASM [2], and custom recordings. It provides continuous, dense segmentation masks paired with comprehensive state graphs that explicitly link parts as they separate and merge over time. By modeling multi-stage assemblies and disassemblies and more than doubling the annotated transformations of prior work [29], VISTA provides highly realistic testbed for dynamic environments (see Appendix C.1 for the detailed dataset composition and Appendix C.2 for the complete annotation protocol). Discussion. Prior metrics [29] evaluate transformations through their temporal boundaries, using precision (T TAS ) and recall (T TAS ), and through the spatial overlap of the resulting objects, using HST . These measures capture whether transformation is detected at the correct time and whether its outputs are accurately localized. However, they do not directly assess whether those outputs are correctly associated with the input objects from which they originate. prediction may therefore achieve accurate temporal boundaries and high output overlap while still linking the resulting objects to the wrong inputs, leaving the input-to-output transition itself unevaluated (see Appendix C.3). This is serious weakness of previous evaluation frameworks, as even simple baseline (AlwaysPredict) that predicts disassembly at every mask split and an assembly at every mask overlap (with IoU > 0.5) outperforms state-of-the-art methods such as TubeletGraph in HST on VOST-TAS by predicting 14 to 15 more transformations (Tab. 3). In contrast, our metrics leverage the dense annotations of VISTA to verify the full predicted state graph, including the link between each transformations input and output objects. 4. Since VOST-TAS annotates only the resulting parts of each transformation, TF1 cannot be computed on it, and its TAS metrics reward over-predicting (Tab. 3). We therefore report the full VOST-TAS [29] comparison in Appendix E.2. We further compare against vanilla SAM and two baselines built on the same trackers. The Agentic baseline gives the MLLM (Qwen 3.5 35B) direct control over the tracker through tool-based harness with offline access to the full video (implem. details in Appendix E.1). On VISTA, TIPO achieves state-of-the-art transformation tracking while operating up to an order of magnitude faster. As shown in Tab. 2, both TIPO configurations significantly outperform TubeletGraph across all metrics. By natively handling assemblies and avoiding heavy temporal search, TIPO improves tracking retention (Jtr) by +5.2 points using SAM 2.1. This gap widens drastically in stategraph generation, with absolute gains of +32.2 TF1 points with SAM 2.1 (44.7 vs 12.5) and +39.2 points with SAM 3 (42.5 vs 3.3). This demonstrates that tracker cues alone are insufficient to detect transformations. Notably, the Agentic baseline falls 34.8 and 32.2 TF1 points behind TIPO with the same MLLM, degrades tracking below vanilla SAM, and runs 2.0 and 2.4 slower, despite its access to the full video. On disassemblies alone, TIPO still outperforms TubeletGraph. Since TubeletGraph cannot handle assemblies, we also evaluate on split of VISTA that removes them while keeping all 132 disassemblies (41 clips). Ablation Study Single-point prompts let SAM resolve ambiguity through its own prior. single point is inherently ambiguous: it may belong to sub-part, part, or the whole object. SAM resolves this by selecting the most plausible mask, revealing which object it believes the point belongs to. Ensembling these single-point decodings probes SAMs zero-shot objectness prior without biasing the decoding. Adding points removes this ambiguity: the decoder must cover all prompts, and the mask collapses onto the sampled component. For an occluded object, the decoded mask no longer extends to other fragments, producing spurious disassemblies; for assemblies, merged parts no longer yield overlapping masks. As shown in Tab. 5, sampling = 4 points drops TF1 by 11.7 with the MLLM Judge and 11.3 without it. Both inner and external mask overlaps are strictly required to evaluate state proposals. In Eqs. (6) and (7), we formulated Φin, Ψin and Φex, Ψex as the foundational metrics for assessing assemblies and disassemblies. Tab. 5 demonstrates the critical necessity of external recall (Φex, Ψex). Excluding these terms mathematically blinds the evaluation to whether sub-state incorrectly bleeds into external components, causing performance to collapse by 17.7 TF1 points for assemblies and 15.3 TF1 points for disassemblies. For instance, hand holding pen splits its mask into two components c1, c2 whose sampled masks both cover the whole pen. Inner recall alone then scores the spurious split {{c1}, {c2}} as high as the intact pen {{c1, c2}}, whereas Φex penalizes the leakage of each part into the other. Advanced reasoning models provide precise transformation classification. We evaluate the impact of the MLLM Labeler in populating the final state-graph labels. As shown in Tab. 6, while object naming accuracy (SO) remains relatively stable across most models, action naming (SA) requires deeper temporal understanding. GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.4 mini outperform the best local model by at least +9.8 SA points, while GPT-5.4 delivers the highest overall semantic accuracy and is our default MLLM Labeler. The MLLM Judge substantially improves spatial reasoning, though the Judge-free pipeline remains highly competitive. The MLLM Judge acts as final filter to verify whether the highest-scoring state proposal actually occurred. As shown in Tab. 2, integrating the judge yields definitive improvement of +8.0 to +9.1 TF1 points across trackers. However, achieving over 33.0 TF1 relying solely on mask overlap scoring shows that the Judge-free configuration suits deployments with strict computational constraints. 5. Conclusion We introduced Transformation Tracking and Understanding to generalize video tracking to environments where objects undergo structural changes, unifying assembly and disassembly into continuous state graphs. To benchmark this task, we curated VISTA, featuring 256 densely annotated, multi-step transformations. We also proposed TIPO, training-free framework that replaces reactive spatiotemporal search with continuous, per-frame structural evaluation and MLLM validation. By leveraging the zero-shot priors of modern foundation models, TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy, operating up to an order of magnitude faster than prior work. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of continuous structural modeling for tracking objects in complex, real-world environments.

As detailed in Sec. 3.2, the framework extracts the sampled masks si by prompting the visual decoder with single point (K = 1) drawn from within the spatial boundaries of each disjoint component. While Sec. 3.2 conceptually separates the Tracker and the Mask Decoder, our experiments instantiate both using the same foundation model (e.g., SAM 2.1 or SAM 3) to maximize inference efficiency via feature caching. However, the framework architecture is strictly modular, decoupling temporal tracking from single-frame zero-shot segmentation. This flexibility allows future deployments to pair lightweight, trackingonly model with an independent promptable mask decoder, naturally accommodating advancements in either domain. Algorithmic Bounds for State Generation. As formulated in Sec. 3.2, the State Generator enumerates all possible physical configurations by computing the partition set Π(X) of the tracked objects or disjoint components. Because the cardinality of partition set scales according to the n-th Bell number Bn, an unconstrained search could lead to combinatorial explosion. To ensure computational tractability in our experiments, we set configurable parameter that limits the number of locally interacting items to 7, which limits the search space at B7 = 877 unique state proposals. To further optimize assembly generation, we strictly pre-filter the input space by excluding any objects whose sampled masks do not spatially overlap. Additionally, to avoid very small noisy components in the mask to interfere, we filter each component with area smaller than 0.02% of the image resolution, analogous to TubeletGraph [29]. The measured runtime of state generation and evaluation up to this bound is reported in Appendix D.3. (left) Transformation tracking quality TF1 on VISTA as function of the state selection threshold τ for SAM 2.1 and SAM 3. (right) Frequency with which each threshold is selected across the 100 folds of 10 10-fold cross-validation, using single threshold shared by both trackers. The selected value τ = 0.8 is highlighted. Threshold Selection without MLLM Judge. VISTA does not provide separate labelled validation split. Therefore, to select τ for TIPO w/o Judge without fitting the evaluation sequences, we adopt repeated k-fold crossvalidation over the 50 sequences of VISTA. We sweep τ {0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9} (seed 0) and, for each of 10 repetitions with different random split, we partition the sequences into 10 folds. In each fold, we select the threshold that maximizes the mean TF1 on the 45 training sequences and evaluate it on the 5 held-out ones, for total of 100 selections. Crucially, we do not tune τ for specific tracker: the selection criterion is the TF1 averaged over SAM 2.1 and SAM 3, yielding single threshold shared by both trackers. As shown in Fig. 8 (right), τ = 0.8 is selected in 97 out of 100 folds, and τ = 0.9 in the remaining 3. The sensitivity analysis in Fig. 8 (left) explains this choice: increasing τ from 0.5 to 0.8 improves TF1 by +13.8 and +9.9 points for SAM 2.1 and SAM 3 respectively. Beyond τ = 0.8, SAM 2.1 saturates (+0.8 TF1 points) while SAM 3 drops by 4.0 points, since valid transformations start to be rejected. The selected τ = 0.8 is then frozen and used in all the TIPO w/o Judge experiments. This confirms that single threshold transfers across trackers without any tracker-specific tuning. B.4. Software and Hardware Specifications All experiments, including pure tracking and MLLM inference, were conducted using two NVIDIA A100 64GB GPUs. All methods are implemented and evaluated using Python 3.12.13 and PyTorch 2.7.0 (CUDA 12.6). All open-weight MLLMs and LLMs are self-hosted using vLLM 0.23.0. To improve reproducibility, we set the decoding temperature to 0 for all LLMs and MLLMs whenever the model provider allows it. The default seed is 0 for Python, PyTorch and Numpy random number generators. Multi-seed experiments use seeds {0, 1, 2}. C. The VISTA Benchmark This section expands upon the VISTA benchmark introduced in Sec. 3.3. First, we describe the composition of the dataset. Then, we detail the custom annotation pipeline and expert protocol utilized to guarantee high-fidelity groundtruth state graphs for the Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU) task. Finally, we formalize the mathematical definitions for our proposed tracking and state-graph evaluation metrics. C.1. Dataset Composition VISTA comprises 50 video sequences collected from three sources: 17 videos from Assembly101 [27], 8 videos from IKEA ASM [2], and 25 custom recordings. The sequences cover diverse set of object categories, including generic household objects (e.g., USB sticks, perfume boxes, moka pots, mixers, remote controls, and digital cameras), IKEA furniture (e.g., tables and drawers), and toy vehicles from Assembly101 (e.g., bulldozers, garbage trucks, and excavators), for total of 218 unique object and part names. The annotated transformations are described by 43 distinct action descriptions, such as disconnect, insert, mount, pop, pull out, put, remove, screw, separate, and unscrew. All annotations have been manually checked and validated by an expert annotator to ensure the temporal and spatial validity of each transformation. C.2. Annotation Protocol and Interface To construct the VISTA dataset, we designed custom annotation interface  (Fig. 9)  that couples automated object tracking with expert human verification. The ground-truth annotations require two modalities: dense spatial masks and discrete state transformations. Masks are generated by an annotator assisted by Promptable Visual Segmentation tracker (SAM 3 [6]), while the transformations are manually logged to construct the ground-truth state graph. Each sequence was annotated by one annotator and independently reviewed by Figure 9. Overview of the VISTA Annotation Tool. Our custom interface couples automated object tracking with expert human verification to construct high-fidelity state graphs. (Top) The landing page features an interactive video player, central tracker controls, and lateral panels for object and graph management. (1) Add Object: The annotator registers new distinct entity ID in the system. (2) Segment and Track: By clicking on the object within the video frame, the annotator prompts the segmentation model to extract the spatial mask and initiates temporal tracking. (3) Log Transformation: At the exact frame of physical state change, the expert opens dialog box to explicitly link the preand post-transformation object tracks and assign semantic action label (e.g., Unscrew). (4) Transformation Logged: The validated event is immediately committed to the state graph and displayed in the right-hand panel for continuous review. second; disagreements on transformation timing, structure, or labels were discussed and resolved until both agreed. Registering and Tracking Entities. The annotator initiates the process by defining new object identity and clicking the target within the interactive video player. They then trigger the visual tracker for that specific item (Fig. 9.1, Fig. 9.2). To ensure rigorous structural definitions, the human expert is explicitly tasked with identifying the precise moment transformation is visually completed. Interpreting performance on VOST-TAS requires understanding the critical structural flaws of its evaluation protocol: first, VOST-TAS annotates only the resulting parts at the end frame of each transformation without modeling the state graph; second, its primary metric HST is strictly recall-based and verifies spatial overlap only at the final frame of the ground-truth window, completely blind to which input objects participated in the event. As demonstrated in Tab. 3, this flawed formulation heavily rewards blind over-prediction: the AlwaysPredict baseline achieves the highest HST (13.9 and 15.7) simply by firing spurious disassemblies at every mask split, despite disastrous temporal precision of 6.29.0 TAS . This metric distortion explains the apparent disparity between TubeletGraph and TIPO under SAM 2.1. VOST was specifically collected to induce catastrophic tracker failures through extreme blur and heavy object deformation [30]. Because TubeletGraph detects transformations by interpreting track loss as structural split, it is artificially rewarded on VOST when weaker tracker (SAM 2.1) frequently drops tracks, allowing its reactive tubelet search to trigger and accumulate unpenalized recall credit on HST . In contrast, TIPO evaluates geometry proactively and refuses to predict transformations unless coherent disjoint components and mask priors support them. On severe visual artifacts where SAM 2.1 collapses, TIPO conservatively suppresses false positives, yielding low HST (2.2) solely because the metric fails to penalize TubeletGraphs hallucinated proposals. Then, we present additional qualitative results on VISTA and analyze the failure cases of TIPO. Finally, we discuss the current limitations of our approach. Non-rigid Transformations. While VISTA is designed around assemblies and disassemblies of rigid objects and does not specifically target non-rigid ones, neither the TTU formulation nor TIPO is limited to rigid transformations. Since state proposals are generated and evaluated directly from the tracked masks, no assumption is made on the shape of the involved objects. Fig. 15 shows an example from VOST-TAS (sequence 3511_unscrew_jar_1) with SAM 3 as base tracker. TIPO correctly detects the cap being unscrewed from the jar and, crucially, the sauce squeezed onto the pasta as new, highly deformable entity, whose mask matches the ground truth with an IoU of 0.92 at the end of the transformation. Notably, the masks of the cap and of the sauce are temporarily lost during the video (e.g., while the pasta is being stirred), yet both objects retain their identity once they reappear and no spurious transformation is introduced. This confirms that TIPO does not require uninterrupted tracks, since structural changes are evaluated directly from the available masks rather than triggered by track loss. The example also exhibits the failure modes discussed below. While the sauce is still flowing out of the jar, the tracker repeatedly splits and re-merges the two masks, producing four spurious transformations, and the MLLM Labeler assigns generic names to some states (e.g., the jar is initially labeled as bottle cap). Additional Qualitative Results and Failure Cases. Fig. 16 presents additional qualitative results on VISTA, illustrating successful multi-step assemblies, while Fig. 17 shows two disassemblies from the Assembly101 [27] subset. While TIPO handles these sequences robustly, these examples also highlight specific failure modes stemming from our direct reliance on upstream foundation models. First, the MLLM Labeler occasionally struggles with fine-grained semantics. Without external context (e.g., an instruction manual), visually ambiguous components are often assigned generic labels, such as identifying isolated IKEA drawer parts simply as blocks (Fig. 16, top row). Second, segmentation and tracking errors propagate directly into the state graph. As seen in Fig. 17, the base tracker occasionally drops small parts (e.g., screws or wheels) immediately following disassembly. Furthermore, the bottom row of Fig. 17 illustrates hallucinated transformation caused by segmentation artifact: the tracker merges screwdriver into the toy truck mask. Because TIPO relies on these masks to generate state proposals, this forces an unnecessary structural update in the graph, even though the MLLM Judge correctly recognizes them as separate entities. Limitations. As illustrated by the failure cases above, the accuracy of TIPO is bounded by the quality of the base tracker, the promptable mask decoder, and the reasoning capabilities of the MLLMs. part dropped by the tracker or segmentation artifact can lead to missed or spurious transformation, and visually ambiguous parts can receive generic labels. Moreover, since TIPO operates in an online, streaming fashion, the state graph is built causally, and transformation cannot be revised retroactively once later frames are observed. This property is shared by prior work, in fact, TubeletGraph [29] also processes videos in streaming fashion. Rather than recovering lost tracks, it tracks all candidate regions of the scene as tubelets and decides whether to include them in the state graph after transformation, without ever correcting the transformations already added to the predicted state graph. Crucially, in TIPO an error in the state graph does not propagate to the rest of the video. Although wrong transformation remains in the graph, subsequent state proposals are evaluated directly from the available masks, allowing TIPO to return to state consistent with the observed scene. As shown in Fig. 15, objects whose masks are temporarily lost retain their identity once they reappear and, despite the four spurious transformations caused by the flowing sauce, the objects present at the end of the video are correctly identified. As shown in Tab. 14, TIPO identifies the objects present on the last frame with precision of 93.4, outperforming TubeletGraph by +30.1 F1 points (Appendix D.5). The remaining gap lies in recall (56.7), mostly due to small parts that are not picked up by the tracker during transformation. Promising directions to address these limitations include an offline variant of TIPO that exploits future frames to revise past transformations, and the re-detection of parts missed during transformation to close the recall gap. Finally, as discussed in Sec. 4.1, the direct dependence on foundation models is also fundamental strength. By continuously evaluating structural proposals directly from the raw tracker outputs, rather than relying on reactive and failure-triggered search heuristics, TIPO is uniquely positioned to scale synergistically. As future vision and language foundation models improve in robustness, our framework will naturally and automatically inherit those gains without requiring architectural changes.
